overview: This file contains a December 1938 State Department memorandum and the underlying report by American Consul Gerald Warner on the Taiwan Development Company, a semi-official corporation controlled by the Japanese colonial government in Taiwan. The documents describe plans to raise its capitalization dramatically, expand agriculture, mining, chemicals, fishing, transport, and manufacturing within Taiwan, and use subsidiaries to advance Japanese economic penetration of South China and the wider “South Seas.” They provide detailed information on corporate ownership, capital, production plans, shipping routes, migrant labor, and projects in China, French Indochina, British Malaya, North Borneo, Siam, and the Philippines, while emphasizing the connection between the company’s expansion, Japanese military victories, and imperial economic policy.

subfiles.title: State Department memorandum on the Taiwan Development Company
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: A concise departmental summary of Gerald Warner’s report on the Taiwan Development Company’s capitalization, subsidiaries, and expansion into South China and Southeast Asia.
subfiles.summary: Memo: the government-controlled Taiwan Development Company, capitalized at ¥18.75 million but planning ¥150 million, added salt, mineral, livestock, vehicle, and cotton subsidiaries and pursued overseas projects in Fujian, Indochina, Malaya, Borneo, and Philippine shipping, as a leading tool of Japanese economic expansion.

subfiles.title: Activities of Taiwan Development Company and Its Subsidiaries
subfiles.about: A detailed report on the Taiwan Development Company as an instrument of Japanese domestic, colonial, and overseas economic expansion.
subfiles.summary: Warner reports that Japanese authorities expected the Taiwan Development Company to direct economic development in occupied South China, while the Fukudai Koshi would concentrate on Fujian. He describes the company’s financial position, projected capitalization above ¥150,000,000, domestic projects in power, cement, chemicals, agriculture, livestock, salt, refining, motor vehicles, cotton, and fisheries, and its numerous subsidiary investments. The overseas survey covers trade and factory proposals at Amoy, mineral interests in French Indochina, Johor, and Terengganu, Formosan settlement at Tawau, shipping between Takao and Aparri, and the acquisition of the Kinrei Maru for ore and coal transport. Warner concludes that the semi-official company reflected Japanese government and military policy and had become increasingly important after Japan’s victories in China.

interest: Shows a Taiwan state corporation combining investment, migration, shipping, and wartime strategy across East/Southeast Asia.
